ateret-zekenim/8:א: (א) Permitted to marry a woman on Purim. {Rama: And some say one may not marry on Purim, neither on the 14th nor on the 15th, so as not to mix his joy with Purim joy (Mordechai and Beit Diniya in responsum of Mahari Weil in Hagahah).}
ateret-zekenim/8:ב: (ב) And likewise wearing shaatnez, which is d'rabbanan. {Rama: There too it is good to be stringent and serve God with joy and to be joyful with trembling.}
baer-heitev/1:ב: (ב) To write. Scripture verses and a letter of peace and reminding him of his debts, and likewise anything not requiring great study. Mateh Moshe, Beit Yosef, Orach Chayyim.
baer-heitev/3:_: In eulogy. A place where the custom is that on the seventh day they go to the grave to lament — it is forbidden on Purim except the mourner alone goes there with one chazan and he says hashkavah to him. Even on erev Purim it is forbidden to go there lest people think mourning ceased because of Purim. R' Shimon Halevi siman 13, Knesset HaGedolah.
baer-heitev/4:א: (א) To hear. It requires study, for Rabi did not rule in Sefer HaZekhirim that he not leave his house — if so he should have written in the language of "some say" etc. Magen Avraham.
baer-heitev/4:ג: (ג) In private. He prays in his house and afterward goes to the synagogue to hear Megillah — Tur and so in Levush; however it implies in Tur that in the morning he goes to the synagogue for prayer — see Yoreh Deah siman 393. Magen Avraham. Taz wrote: it appears to me that since there is no mourning on Purim in public, one should not read in the synagogue on Motzei Shabbat before Barchu to walk opposite the mourner, for one should not mention the mourner's name in public; rather he goes to the synagogue without reading — end of his words.
baer-heitev/8:א: (א) To marry. Per what R' Shlomo wrote siman 696, we hold like those who say one may not mix joy with joy — here too it is forbidden; therefore he should make the canopy on the 13th — Magen Avraham see there; see Sefer Gufei Halachot and what is written in Even HaEzer siman 62 s.k. 10.
beer-hagolah/6:_: Tur in name of Maharam of Rothenburg, and so Shach in his name.
beur-hagra/4:ב: (ב) Nevertheless. He disputes Shulchan Aruch in seif 5. His reason: since we say there three [things] that cancel avodah which is d'oraisa, all the more mourning which is d'rabbanan is overridden; and even though in siman 687 seif 2 it is written specifically to precede but not to defer — behold there it is written a d'oraisa mitzvah.
beur-hagra/4:ד: (ד) And some say there is no [mourning]. It is said of them feasting and joy, and they said the the Name: the two days of Purim etc. were needed only to forbid eulogy and liken to professional lamentation. And this is what is written there 3:2 and an individual is light etc. all the more etc. And superficially it is not understood; see Tosafot there s.v. all the more etc. who strained on this and their words are strained, for Megillah is not mentioned there at all, and also all the more is not relevant, and furthermore it says Chanukah — rather according to its plain sense regarding eulogy it speaks: that even though it is written in it feasting and joy and it challenges that just as they cancel avodah because of Torah study, so too remembrance, for they are equated and its essence is avodah, as we wrote 2:2; and in this verse of mishpacha u'mishpacha they are remembered and done as written, and just as they cancel for remembrance, so too for avodah, as we wrote 7:2: the lamp and the rabbis did not come etc. except that it is not relevant to say they cancel avodah, for the whole day is the time of avodah, unlike reading where the zealous etc. — therefore it is clear that feasting and joy of Purim is not deferred except because of Torah scholar before him, as we wrote honor of Torah because of honor of Torah alone.
beur-hagra/4:ה: (ה) And even. Per Tosafot' view that even the first day is d'rabbanan, for they did not say aninut of day one is d'oraisa except in kodashim and maaser; and they brought proof from first chapter of Ketubot daf 4a that mourning is deferred because of the canopy, and in Bechorot 49; and regarding etc. that we hold halacha etc. even the first day; see above siman 688 seif 3 and Yoreh Deah siman 399 seif 13.
beur-hagra/8:א: (א) Permitted to marry. For they said only festival, and derive from scripture "and you shall rejoice in your festival" etc.; and even for those who say one may not mix — it does not apply to the law. Darkei Moshe.
beur-hagra/8:ב: (ב) And all the more permitted. For even on a festival it is permitted as Tosafot wrote there s.v. because of cancellation, for we hold like Rav Ashi who expounds in first chapter of Chagigah "in your festival" and not "with your wife" etc.; and it appears to me they do not count as joy except the wedding feast alone.
beur-hagra/8:ד: (ד) And some forbid. For he wrote: granted money is given for forgiveness, unlike prohibition; and also in wearing to pass etc. Rambam and Shulchan Aruch Yoreh Deah siman 301 seif 5 forbid, see there, and there seif 6 in Hagahah.
chatam-sofer/4:_: (there s.k. 18) except he seized the gemara's language. NB in Chemed Moshe he challenged Rashba: it should be permitted to marry on Shavuot festival day since it is one day — and he forgot that we do not marry women on Yom Tov, for it is like acquiring acquisition as above siman 339 and in Magen Avraham there s.k. 5 and in Shulchan Aruch Even HaEzer siman 64; and the gemara in Moed Katan refers to the week of marriage and not Yom Tov itself, and this is simple.
chokhmat-shlomo/4:_: Seif 4 in Hagahah: nevertheless he goes to synagogue to hear Megillah etc. NB I was in doubt regarding a woman — what is her law, whether she is permitted to go to synagogue to hear Megillah. What brought me to this doubt is per what a certain scholar aroused me to explain for him Rashba's responsum general 27 law 2, who wrote: and a mourner does not leave his house's door the first Shabbat to hear blessing of milah and blessing of bridegrooms; and this that is difficult for you, that a mourner is obligated in all mitzvot stated in Torah — this refers to positive mitzvot in his body such as tzitzit and tefillin or to circumcise his son; but to go to milah and canopy and to hear the blessing for the sake of gemilut chasadim he has no permission to leave his house's door — end of his words. [Brought in Shach Yoreh Deah siman 393 see there.] On this the aforementioned scholar asked: from what is written regarding Megillah, explicit here that he is permitted to go hear Megillah — per the questioner's words now. Behold at first glance it appeared to me to settle that Rashba's intent is specifically where the mitzvah is in action, such as putting on tefillin and the like — then he is permitted to go even though he nullifies mourning, since mourning is all its prohibition in shev v'lo taaseh d'rabbanan, and behold for a Torah prohibition too a positive mitzvah overrides a negative — all the more for d'rabbanan of action which is stronger; unlike hearing blessings and the like which are not action in his body — therefore anything without action in a Torah prohibition is not overridden, and the same for d'rabbanan, for whatever the rabbis enacted they enacted like d'oraisa. Therefore regarding Megillah, since here each is obligated to read Megillah and what one discharges another is by agency, as Peri Megadim wrote in Orach Chayyim and in Sefer Kaf HaChayyim, and I extended on this elsewhere — if so here, since the essence of the mitzvah is obligation on his body in action, only the agent acts and it is as him — if so here there is action, similar to tzitzit and tefillin etc. Per this it appears this is specifically for a male, for the obligation is upon him to read Megillah and what one discharges another is by agency — therefore there is action and mourning is deferred. But for a woman, since she is not obligated in reading only in hearing — if so whoever hears fulfills and she needs no agency at all — here it is like hearing blessings and mourning is not deferred; therefore she is forbidden to go out to hear Megillah since there is no action in her body. So it appeared to him. However in truth there is no proof from this to say one may not learn from Megillah reading because of other things — for behold even Torah study is canceled to hear Megillah reading, and many Torah mitzvot are deferred before Megillah reading; therefore mourning too is deferred before Megillah reading. On the contrary I wonder at those who forbid below in Shulchan Aruch for a mourner to leave his house to hear Megillah; and even those who permit here — nevertheless Rama wrote if possible to gather a minyan at home it is preferable. And why should it be so — behold Torah study, which is stringent, is canceled to hear Megillah reading, and it is clear in poskim that even if possible to read afterward in ten, nevertheless they cancel in order to hear in public. If so, if Torah study which is stringent is canceled, all the more mourning which is lighter; behold this kal vachomer itself they learned in gemara for Torah from avodah: if avodah which is stringent is canceled, Torah which is lighter — not all the more; if so this kal vachomer one may learn all the more regarding mourning which is lighter than Torah and avodah — requires study. Behold in the body of the aforementioned questioner's difficulty on the aforementioned Rashba — from what is written regarding Megillah, in any case it is not difficult, since in Shulchan Aruch there are several views whether a mourner may leave his house — one may say Rashba truly holds he does not leave his house even to hear Megillah. However one who is exacting in Rashba's responsum language will see his intent is thus: the distinction is between whether the essence of the mitzvah depends on his body, such as tzitzit, tefillin, milah where the essence depends on his body — for these we say we defer mourning before them; but a matter not done by him alone only with others' combination, such as hearing milah blessing or canopy blessing — if others were not doing the mitzvah he would have no obligation at all, and the mitzvah is not the essence of his body's obligation, only if others do the mitzvah he too is obligated to go with them to repay kindness — for this we do not defer mourning. If so automatically no question from Megillah, for there whether for men or women the obligation depends on each person's body by himself, either to read Megillah or to hear — therefore we defer mourning before them. Behold what I challenged above — why the mourner does not go hear Megillah from avodah and Torah — here one could say thus per what is written siman 232 and siman 231: one distinguishes between he began in permission and does not stop, and he began in prohibition and stops for all; if so here too what kohanim in their avodah and leviim on the platform cancel their avodah, and likewise the yeshiva of the house of Rabbi — this is when he began on Purim itself at the time the reading obligation already applied to him, therefore they are obligated to cancel; but if he began in permission he does not stop; if so mourning that applied to him before Purim — since this mourning obligation applied before Megillah — he does not stop from mourning to read Megillah. Per this it would appear if mourning did not apply to him except on Purim itself, such as buried on Purim night and the like — then for all he is permitted to go hear Megillah even if he can gather a minyan at home, nevertheless he goes to hear in public, even for those who hold mourning applies on Purim too. So it appeared to me now — requires study. Behold as I speak on this I will mention what arose in my thought to challenge on what we say in gemara there in Megillah: R' Yehoshua ben Levi said a person must read Megillah at night and repeat it by day, as written "so that Your glory may sing and not be silent" etc.; he thought the baraita of daytime helps; a certain rabbi told him etc. like one who passes this portion and teaches it; it is difficult — from R' Yehoshua ben Levi's language it implies his emphasis is on daytime that he is obligated to read also by day; if the emphasis were on night and by day it would be obvious to him — he should have said a person must read Megillah also at night; and since he said a person must read Megillah at night and repeat by day, it implies his main emphasis is on daytime. Difficult on daytime — why did he need the verse "so that Your glory may sing" etc.; and in particular how could he think from it the baraita of daytime, but hold reading obligation is not by day, and how did it enter his mind to say so? Behold since it is written mishpacha u'mishpacha we learn kohanim in their avodah and leviim on the platform and Israel in their maamad cancel their avodah to hear Megillah reading — at night there is no platform and no maamad, per force it deals with daytime reading — if so proven reading is by day. Also from kohanim in their avodah one could challenge: even though burning limbs is valid all night, nevertheless since we wrote it is proven from poskim' words that where another mitzvah applied to him before Megillah it is not deferred before Megillah — if so per force what kohanim cancel in their avodah is by day when this obligation applied to them together with Megillah, unlike burning limbs at night that applied to them from day 13 before Megillah obligation. If so one may learn kal vachomer: if mourning is not deferred before Megillah, all the more avodah which is stringent; per force it does not deal with nighttime when there is no avodah, only what remains of the day; if so per force it deals from daytime — and how could it enter his mind there is no Megillah reading by day — requires study now — requires study well. (there in that seif in Hagahah) And some say mourning does not apply on Purim, neither on the 14th nor on the 15th etc. NB from this I learned another new law regarding shmuah kerovah on Purim that in the end becomes distant — its law as explicit in Shulchan Aruch and in Shulchan Aruch Yoreh Deah siman 402: shmuah kerovah on Shabbat that in the end becomes distant — he practices only one hour; explicit there in Beit Yosef in name of Rashba's responsum the reason: even though mourning applies on Shabbat and counts even at its beginning — nevertheless here it is different, for mourning does not apply afterward except from Shabbat force while it is still the thirty-day day; if so the secondary should not be more stringent than it, for in it mourning does not apply yet its cause causes mourning — see there; if so here too since on Purim mourning does not apply, the cause should not be more stringent. Per this it appears further: even if Purim occurred after Shabbat and it is the thirty-day day on Purim and he was informed on Shabbat too — he does not have the law of shmuah kerovah, for his law is like hearing inside the festival and after the festival becomes distant. Superficially one could distinguish and say on a festival properly he has the law of distant shmuah, since on a festival mourning did not apply to him, for festival does not count in the seven — if so necessarily now mourning did not apply to him, and after the festival at the hour mourning began on him it was already distant — therefore he has distant shmuah law even though still within the thirty-day day itself. On Shabbat, even though Shabbat counts and mourning applies to him — nevertheless since on Shabbat it deals with the thirty-day day itself, and such since it is the last day and we hold part of the day is like the whole — if so if he already knew the matter mourning was already ceased from him, only that since he still did not know his law is like the day before — therefore enough to be stringent if mourning applied immediately; but if now it is Shabbat and mourning did not apply for all its laws, they were not stringent to be like the day before, and we say in it part of the day is like the whole. But if he was informed on Shabbat that within the thirty days only immediately adjacent to Shabbat is Purim, a festival on which mourning does not apply in eating, and afterward it became distant — here properly he has shmuah kerovah law, since he was informed within thirty days itself and Shabbat counts in the seven — nevertheless per Rashba's responsum reason that the secondary should not be more stringent than itself, it appears there is no distinction in the matter, and in every case mourning ceases from him since afterward it will not apply except from Shabbat force and the secondary will not be more stringent. And truthfully, without Rashba's words it would appear the reason of the matter of shmuah kerovah on Shabbat and after festival becomes distant — he practices only one hour — we were because the reason of shmuah kerovah is the day of hearing is as if before him. Therefore it appears this is specifically on a day that if he died now aninut of the first day would apply, whether before burial or after burial; therefore here it is relevant to say the day of hearing is as if before him. But on Shabbat and festival, if he died for him now aninut law after burial would not apply, as Rashba wrote in Laws of Chol HaMoed: if the first day is on Chol HaMoed he puts on tefillin — even disputants there, it is for another reason, for otherwise Chol HaMoed is not the main time of tefillin; but otherwise they would agree — if so the stringency of day one after burial did not apply to him, therefore when the essence is nullified the secondary is nullified too. But on Purim, since aninut applies to him by law — and even for those who permit meat and wine, this is only from communal positive mitzvah force, but from tefillin certainly exempt on day one even on Purim — since aninut of day one after burial applied to him, the secondary applied too; unlike Shabbat and festival, if tefillin mitzvah were relevant they would put on tefillin and would not be exempt from tefillin law from aninut after burial — if so since stringency of one day applied to him, the secondary applied too. In any case it appears since halacha follows the lenient in mourning, one may rely on Rashba's reason, especially since my ruling does not decide against Rashba's words even as a drop from the sea. Per Rashba's reason, on Purim too it is so like Shabbat; in particular since in Rama's language here Purim is mentioned like Shabbat, and also Beit HaGadol's view that Purim's law is like festivals that interrupt and do not count at all — in this and this certainly woe if his law were like shmuah kerovah on festival that after festival becomes distant that he practices only one day; therefore in this law there is doubt perhaps like Beit HaGadol and Purim's law is like festivals. And if you say not like Beit HaGadol — perhaps like Rashba's reason; if so even if his law is like Shabbat, here it is like distant shmuah law. Therefore one may rely on the halacha as written, especially in mourning d'rabbanan. So it appeared to me clear for the law — requires study well. May God repair breaches with us Israel and swallow death forever and make us rejoice in His salvation; we end with holy Rama's words end of siman 697: good heart, joy always. I present here what I said in my chiddushim on Orach Chayyim year 5549 on what is brought above siman 695: a person must become intoxicated on Purim until he does not know between arur Haman and baruch Mordechai. It appears as a new matter: behold Chazal said per one view that therefore we do not say Hallel on Purim — we do not say song on a miracle outside the land. It appears this is explicit in the words of the psalmist David who said "Who will give from Zion salvation of Israel — Jacob will exult, Israel will rejoice" — behold the essence of song is said on joy, and if there is no joy there is no song; therefore he said "Who will give from Zion salvation of Israel." If salvation were from Zion, meaning Eretz Yisrael, then Jacob would exult, Israel would rejoice; but if salvation is outside the land and not from Zion, Israel has no joy in it and there is no song. Therefore it appears also for the other view that gemara concludes in Arachin that its reading is its Hallel — since they were exiled they returned to the first permission; nevertheless they made a distinction that a miracle of chutz la'aretz and Eretz Yisrael are not equal. Therefore they enacted on Purim feasting and joy in remembrance of feasting first; and on all Yom Tov we find only mitzvah of joy and not feasting — this is like they enacted on Purim to divide honor to Eretz Yisrael in enactment of walled cities as Ran wrote; so they enacted further that all festivals made for Israel in Eretz Yisrael or before their coming to Eretz Yisrael when all lands are equal — joy alone is relevant; but on Purim when they had already merited Eretz Yisrael before, it would be fitting not to rejoice at all on a miracle in chutz la'aretz. Therefore when they enacted joy they enacted feasting first, so joy not be from the miracle alone but also from feasting, as is the way of all who drink — his heart rejoices — and joy also through feasting, to show feasting too causes joy, and we have no complete joy since the miracle was in chutz la'aretz and not of Eretz Yisrael — therefore feasting and afterward joy. From this reason too, though they enacted to read Megillah which is in place of Hallel for us who hold its reading is its Hallel — nevertheless they enacted likewise to become intoxicated on Purim until he does not know between arur Haman etc., so he forget to say the song since its reading is its Hallel. If so proven telling the miracle is the Hallel; if so automatically what is said arur Haman and baruch Mordechai is also Hallel and song; therefore obligated to become intoxicated until he does not know between arur Haman etc., so the song not be in his mouth all day and song not be complete, since it is a miracle in chutz la'aretz our joy in it is not complete — therefore song too will not be complete all day, only he forget it; unlike a miracle in Eretz Yisrael of which it is said "When God returns Zion's captivity" — when the miracle is in Eretz Yisrael then our mouth will be filled with laughter and our tongue with rinnah all day, and we will not need to drink to forget the song, only "my tongue shall speak Your righteousness all day, Your glory" — and song will be complete. So may it be with God's help, amen, speedily and in our days, and may the redeemer come to Zion speedily in our days, amen and amen.
eliyah-rabbah/2:_: [2] [Levush] Some say one must etc. End of siman 679 he ruled thus in stam, and Rama wrote one should permit his vow, and so ruled Shach in Yoreh Deah siman 295; and the same law on Rosh Chodesh and Chanukah; see end of siman 318.
kaf-hachayyim/3:_: (3) there. One does not do [melacha]. Through a gentile it is permitted. Magen Avraham s.k. 1. Eliyah Rabbah s.k. 1. Even HaEzer s.k. 1. Orach Chayyim s.k. 1. Chayei Adam general rule 135 s.k. 34. Mishna Berurah s.k. 2. And likewise when he has nothing to eat, it is permitted to do melacha and sew his friend's garments for wages, for all this is joy for him. Even HaEzer there. Mishna Berurah in Sefer HaTzavaot letter 2; and likewise if there is loss in the matter it is permitted, for anything of joy is permitted on Purim. Mateh Zion s.k. 1. Mishna Berurah in Sefer HaTzavaot s.k. 3.
kaf-hachayyim/4:_: (4) One who was building his house before Purim through a gentile — since the matter became known, he should stop on Purim day. Beit Din siman 695. Birkei Yosef s.k. 3. Orach Chayyim there Shaarei Teshuvah s.k. 1. And in Sefer Chok LeYisrael vol. 2 Yoreh Deah in remnants of Orach Chayyim siman 20 he permitted building a shop on the 14th and 15th and acted thus — see there; building a synagogue and a matter of mitzvah is permitted. Rokeach 1:10:1 and in his book Malach siman 31 s.k. 31.
kaf-hachayyim/5:_: (5) there in Hagahah. And nowadays they practiced everywhere not to do. It appears merchandise is permitted since it is joy for him. Taz s.k. 1. And so Knesset HaGedolah in Hagahot Beit Yosef s.k. 5, except he wrote: even though we liken to it, we do not make an act to permit commerce on Purim in a place that practiced not to do melacha — but if one transgressed and did, bet din does not fine him unless they made a fence lest people breach in doing melacha; all this depends on the appearance to bet din's eyes — see there. And so Shulchan Gavoah s.k. 3; it appears if bet din sent to warn him not to trade and he did not heed, bet din may put him in nidui. Rokeach s.k. 2; see above siman 554 seif 22 and in our words there b'siyata dishmaya.
kaf-hachayyim/7:_: (7) there. He does not see a sign of blessing etc. — it implies a sign of blessing is what is not fitting; behold we call him and do not put him in cherem for him; and so is the view of most poskim; but Rav Acha Gaon in Sheiltot — Hagahot Maimoniot and Razah in Sefer HaMaor and in Orach Chayyim wrote we put him in cherem. Birkei Yosef s.k. 5. Orach Chayyim s.k. 2. For the matter of practice he agreed in Knesset HaGedolah (in Hagahot Beit Yosef end s.k. 2) that nowadays they practiced everywhere not to do, and if one did they do not put him in cherem and do not fine him, only he does not see a sign of blessing. Shulchan Gavoah s.k. 4.
kaf-hachayyim/8:_: (8) It appears to me that even for a Jew they fine only one who does melacha b'mezid; but b'shogeg when he thought melacha was permitted they do not punish him, for shogeg is not like mezid. Knesset HaGedolah there s.k. 3. And if he is b'mezid, even though they do not put him in nidui since it is doubtful in the dispute of poskim — nevertheless they may fine him, for all he profited from that melacha he gives to the poor, all per the judge's view. Rokeach s.k. 3. And so in his book Malach siman 31 s.k. 34.
levushei-serad/4:_: s.k. 4 to go to synagogue. Before Barchu, for Shabbat sanctity is still upon him; but after Barchu he returns home — unlike here, since on Purim in Rama's words, if he went before Barchu he will be there after prayer and Megillah as if he were in the synagogue from the outset; unlike on a weekday he must pray Maariv at home and afterward go to synagogue as Magen Avraham wrote in s.k. 8.
levushei-serad/7:_: s.k. 12 his law is like Shabbat. For the law of portions is like the law of asking peace, and he wrote there on the 14th in s.k. 3 that on Shabbat there are places that permit asking peace of a mourner and there are places that forbid — therefore in places that practiced permission, portions too are permitted — see there; and the same here on Purim, whose law is also like Shabbat regarding mourning: portions are permitted in a place where they practice permission to ask peace on Shabbat, for according to them it is likewise permitted to ask peace on Purim — therefore portions too are permitted. But Taz s.k. 3 understood Rama's intent here on what Rama wrote there in s.k. 2 that nowadays they are lenient in asking peace of a mourner after thirty days and there is no reason for this unless we say the peace we practice is not called asking peace as in their days — see there; therefore Taz was puzzled on portions, there is no such permission — therefore he wrote one should not rely on this etc.; but per Magen Avraham's explanation there is no difficulty, for Rama's intent is to permit portions on Purim in places that permit on Shabbat asking peace of a mourner, for he holds that even asking peace as in their days was permitted on Shabbat — simple.
levushei-serad/8:_: Magen Avraham s.k. 13 as written siman 688 seif 3. For individual d'oraisa positive mitzvah, namely mourning day one, overrides communal d'rabbanan positive mitzvah, namely joy of two festival days — if so, here too aninut to forbid meat and wine is d'rabbanan and is deferred before Purim which is d'oraisa positive mitzvah; and all the more since it is also communal positive mitzvah — therefore one need not give the reason that mourning is individual positive mitzvah.
machatzit-hashekel/1:_: (s.k. 1) In all places Orach Chayyim 568 — through a gentile it is permitted on erev Purim, all the more on Purim which is lighter. For one who does melacha on erev Purim they put him in cherem; one who does on Purim they do not put him in cherem.
machatzit-hashekel/2:ב: (ב) But in Beit Yosef it implies etc., that he wrote Rambam's proof is from the incident of Rav who saw that man sowing flax on Purim; and he erred and the flax did not sprout — behold it appears he does not see a sign of blessing. If so there is no proof except for a place that practiced prohibition, for the gemara there challenges on what it concludes there that prohibition of melacha was not accepted and it is permitted by law — if so why did Rav curse that man? And they answer: because of things permitted and others practiced prohibition on them. If so necessarily in the place where that man sowed there was a place that practiced prohibition on it, and in a place that did not practice prohibition there is no proof that he does not see a sign of blessing.
machatzit-hashekel/8:_: (s.k. 8) Matters etc.; however it implies in Tur etc. that he wrote: and after he prays in the mourner's house on the night of Purim he goes to synagogue to hear — nevertheless end of his words. And from that he wrote on the night of Purim it implies specifically at night before prayer Purim had not yet begun — so too; but by day he is permitted to go to synagogue to pray.
magen-avraham/1:א: (א) In all places. Orach Chayyim 568 that through a gentile it is permitted; see siman 554 s.k. 22.
magen-avraham/3:_: Forbidden in eulogy. A place where the custom is that on the seventh day they go to the grave to lament — forbidden on Purim except the mourner alone goes there with one chazan and says hashkavah to him; even on erev Purim it is forbidden to go there lest people think mourning ceased because of Purim (R' Shimon Levi 13, Knesset HaGedolah).
magen-avraham/4:א: (א) Nevertheless he goes to synagogue. It requires study, for Rabi ruled in Sefer HaZekhirim that he not leave his house — if so he should have written in the language of "some say" etc.
magen-avraham/4:ב: (ב) And some say there is no mourning etc. Bach and Rashal and Perishah testified the custom is to mourn; and so Maharil; and now the world follows Rama's words; it appears to me one should be careful in all except removing shoes and sitting on the ground because of people, and all the more forbidden to see all kinds of joy.
magen-avraham/4:ג: (ג) Private matters etc. He prays in his house and afterward goes to synagogue to hear Megillah (Tur and so in Levush); however it implies in Tur that in the morning he goes to synagogue for prayer — see Yoreh Deah siman 393.
magen-avraham/7:ב: (ב) And all the more he is obligated. Rama's words require great study: granted in meat and wine it is permitted because of Purim joy; but Shema and prayer — the reason he is exempt is he should be free for the deceased's needs; if so what is different about Purim from weekdays? And even if one says he holds that at night he is obligated in Shema since his law is like second day of Yom Tov as written siman 688 seif 5 — nevertheless it is difficult how we learn this in what he wrote in meat and wine, what relevance does this have to that — requires study.
magen-avraham/7:ג: (ג) Specifically at night. It requires study why he should be permitted at night in meat and wine, for behold there is no obligation at all to eat at night as Rashi wrote siman 695; if so how did he write communal positive mitzvah etc.; and it is puzzling on the 14th siman 341 he ruled that even on Shabbat if he wishes not to eat meat the permission is in his hand, as Terumat HaDeshen wrote: he is not obligated to eat meat and wine etc.; what they forbade on a weekday is lest he continue after his pleasures and be nullified from burying the deceased — end of his words (and see siman 552 seif 10 that when prevented because of mourning it is forbidden); if so there is no positive mitzvah at all even by day; and it is possible to say Purim is different since it is written therein joy, and there is no joy except with meat — nevertheless it is difficult, for Yom Tov too joy is written therein and there is no obligation to eat meat except when the Temple stood — see siman 529; therefore it appears to me at night in any case he should not eat meat, for in any case there is prevention as written siman 695 seif 2 in Hagahah; and what he wrote "it appears to me specifically at night" refers to Megillah.
magen-avraham/8:_: Permitted to marry. On a festival it is written "and you shall rejoice in your festival" and not "with your wife," and not on Purim; and further it is one day, and because of one day a person does not delay himself, and as those who say because of cancellation of procreation (Beit Yosef in name of Rashba); superficially it implies here that granted on a festival we decree lest he delay until the festival to become intoxicated and the seven days of feasting come out on the seven days of the festival — but on Purim because of one day he will not delay — requires study, for we say in gemara it is permitted to marry on erev the festival, for because of one day a person does not delay himself (Rashi and Ran: since if he delays further he cannot do on the festival) — if so he should not set up the marriage on erev the festival, and this is not relevant regarding Purim; and it is possible Rashba's reasoning is he speaks of his own soul alone, only he seized the gemara's language; nevertheless it is difficult from where he learned this, and it is possible his proof is from that it is permitted to marry on erev Shavuot and we are not concerned he will delay the marriage until after Shavuot, for it is only one day — rather per force since it is only one day he is not concerned to delay, for in any case he must do seven days of feasting. Levush wrote per what I wrote siman 688 seif 6 one should not make the Purim feast on Shabbat — if so here too forbidden to make a wedding feast on the 14th per force; in my humble opinion it is not comparable, for there the reason is if so the Purim feast would not be recognizable; but here what matter if the wedding feast is not recognizable; see what I wrote there; but if it is difficult, this is difficult, for we hold one may not mix joy with joy as I wrote beginning siman 696 and we derive from scripture — if so how permitted to mix wedding joy with Purim joy? One could say: therefore Rashba concluded these matters are d'rabbanan and we follow leniency — meaning for those who say one may not mix, in truth it is forbidden; but since for the other view it is permitted, we follow leniency; if so per what I wrote beginning siman 696 we hold like those who say one may not mix joy with joy — here too forbidden; therefore it appears he should make the canopy on the 13th as above.
mechaber/7:main: There are those who say an onen is permitted in meat and wine, for the individual positive mitzvah of mourning does not come and override the communal d'oraisa positive mitzvah of rejoicing on Purim, which are divrei kabbalah and are like Torah law. {Rama: And all the more so he is obligated in Megillah reading and prayer and Shema; it appears to me specifically at night even though the deceased is laid before him, but by day when he wishes to bury him he buries his dead first as explained above siman 687 seif 2, and therefore reads and prays afterward, for Purim is not more important than Yom Tov and Shabbat as explained above siman 71, so it is.}
mishnah-berurah/1:ב: (ב) One does not do — and through a gentile it is permitted.
mishnah-berurah/3:ב: (ט) And fasting — and regarding Torah scholar see above siman 695 seif 2 in Hagahah and in Mishna Berurah there. Law of Torah scholar before him see Yoreh Deah siman 401.
mishnah-berurah/4:א: (י) He goes to synagogue to hear etc. — and what he wrote in seif 5 at the end that the next day he does not leave his house refers when he has a minyan at home, though in general public reading is preferable.
mishnah-berurah/4:ד: (יג) Private matters are practiced — behold Taz wrote walking from his house to prayer is forbidden also per this view, and this is not called in public for it is not recognizable he does so because of mourning; in Magen Avraham he wrote it implies in Tur that in the morning he goes to synagogue to pray; see Peri Megadim who wrote one who is lenient to behave thus did not lose; and so in Darkei Chayyim that in the morning he goes to prayer in synagogue.
mishnah-berurah/5:א: (טו) He does not leave from there etc. — this law Rokeach wrote, and in his place they would eat the third meal before Minchah; therefore he says when he comes to pray Minchah he does not leave from there; but for us he must go home after Minchah to eat the third meal, and at night pray Maariv and read Megillah at home if he has a minyan; and if not, he goes to synagogue while it is still day and is there for prayer and Megillah reading.
mishnah-berurah/5:ב: (טז) From his house's door — only to hear Megillah reading if he has no minyan at home, as above. Behold the Mechaber who copied Rokeach's words follows his view b'siyata dishmaya that mourning applies on Purim; but Rama already wrote above that we practice like poskim that mourning does not apply on Purim; per this, even if he has a minyan at home he goes to synagogue to hear Megillah in public [and to leave his house's door for discretionary matters — it implies from Peri Megadim one should be stringent]; all this by day, for "days of feasting and joy" is written; but at night if he has a minyan he prays and reads Megillah at home, and if not he prays at home and goes to hear Megillah in synagogue, and for reading alone he does not leave his house's door. See Darkei Chayyim that on day 15 he does not go from house to synagogue even for Shacharit prayer; nevertheless regarding removing shoes and sitting on ground it implies from poskim that even on day 15 it is not required. Levush wrote: Orach Chayyim justified the law and does not say Kaddish except before a sage in his presence after they eulogize him; and even though Orach Chayyim 395 they say Kaddish.
mishnah-berurah/6:ו: (ו) Unless the mourner forgives etc. — for one does not give a person a gift against his will.
mishnah-berurah/7:ג: (כה) And all the more he is obligated in Megillah etc. — meaning: just as for the mitzvah of joy of the day we defer the positive mitzvah of mourning and permitted him in meat and wine, certainly it is not fitting to exempt him at night from Megillah and other mitzvot since there is no way to bury then, similar to onen on second day of Yom Tov whom many poskim obligated in mitzvot for this reason; but one may question this: one, that on second night of Yom Tov itself there are views among poskim; another, that there at least it is Yom Tov, therefore aninut does not apply because there is no way to bury at night — unlike Purim whose main joy is by day, and at night is like other weekday nights, certainly aninut applies even if there is no way to bury then; therefore Darkei Chayyim wrote on the night of the 14th he hears Megillah reading afterward.
mishnah-berurah/7:ד: (כו) Burial of his dead first as explained etc. — meaning there it is proven not specifically a mitzvah corpse before Megillah reading — likewise any dead person who has no burying enough for his need, the one encountering him buries him first and then reads. In truth Magen Avraham already wrote many poskim dispute this and hold that for any dead person Megillah reading precedes his burial, and so they practice to bury after leaving synagogue; Magen Avraham challenged: fine for other people, but how is the onen obligated in Megillah reading — behold he is exempt from all mitzvot, and how did he fulfill through what he heard in public after he was not obligated at all? Per force Magen Avraham concludes: even though he heard the reading in public he reads it again after the dead is buried. Regarding Shema and prayer he is like other onen on weekdays: before burial he is exempt, after burial see above siman 71 in Mishna Berurah s.k. 4 there all details are explained. Regarding tefillin, view of many acharonim he does not put them on, as above siman 38 seif 5.
mishnah-berurah/8:ב: (כט) Pidyon haben — and milah, for in these there is not so much joy that one could say one may not mix joy with joy.
peri-megadim/1:א: (א) In every place that they do not do — and in Beit Yosef the word "that" is missing, printing error; and in Darkei Moshe 1 in name of Kol Bo that nowadays they accepted not to do and to forbid this for that — 14th for walled cities etc. — there is no custom even now; and Orach Chayyim beginning ch. 22 of Megillah: it was writing this teaches Purim is permitted in melacha, meaning if by law forbidden one does not distinguish mitzvah or not; but custom alone one could say for mitzvah need; and Piskei Halachot and Megillah permits writing. And there he rejects that it deals with villages — see there. And see siman 568 regarding erev Purim: at night until sunrise it is permitted even if they practiced not to do, and it appears all the more Purim; and the same if there is loss in the matter it is permitted, for anything of joy is permitted on Purim; and in Eshel Avraham he brought Ran's words in Megillah: it was writing Yerushalmi teaches Purim is permitted in melacha on the 14th in walled cities; and Ran z"l explained except the 15th on Shabbat and they read on the 14th etc. — all the more villages that advance entry are permitted in melacha on the day they read; in Magen Avraham we wrote from this in letter 2 — this is reasonable for villages. And Yerushalmi holds one should not distinguish between villages and cities; and it appears he holds not in its time for villages requires ten for delay — how is it relevant he will prepare ten and not intend, unlike cities on the 14th one could say it was its time and need not interpret thus.
peri-megadim/1:ב: (ב) And know what is written in Hagahah "and nowadays they practiced not to do" — Kol Bo likewise in name of Orach Chayyim and Beit HeBad wrote Kol Bo; and Rabbenu Yerucham implies he did not see Beit Yosef's house examination as written in general rules Orach Chayyim on the 14th. Beit Yosef concludes: one who does — they put him in cherem since his prohibition spread in all Israel; in Eliyah Rabbah 1 in name of Knesset HaGedolah they do not put in nidui — requires study. It implies that by custom they do not put in nidui except when his prohibition spread in most of Israel; one city is not custom; see Pesachim 52 in Rashi 5: Yom Tov they put in nidui on Yom Tov even though it is custom — it implies disregard of Yom Tov is why they put in nidui; if not so, custom not spread in all Israel — no; and Orach Chayyim 466 letter 1 s.v. and if it is difficult — see there; and see R' Yehuda Dein siman 61 it implies custom is like a vow — requires study; the matters are long.
peri-megadim/2:_: And some say Orach Chayyim — superficially from Tur who brought Maharam of Rothenburg's words; but on Purim night after praying Maariv at home he goes to synagogue to hear Megillah — one could say specifically Maariv they pray somewhat from the outset, unlike morning he goes to synagogue to pray, for he holds there is no mourning on Purim; and Orach Chayyim 5: but Rosh brought Maharam's language that Beit Yosef brought: there is no mourning on Purim, and after praying Maariv at home he goes to synagogue for Megillah, for Megillah avodah defers it — all the more mourning d'rabbanan; it implies Megillah defers it — behold prayer even morning at home; and it implies also even if he has a minyan at home public reading is preferable like avodah — 13 kohanim gain in tamid, nevertheless in public preferable; Magen Avraham 6; and Eliyah Rabbah there will be explained. Hence private matters are practiced on Purim even without leaving his house's door at all for discretionary matters; and for Taz even for prayer he does not go out, only in public removing shoe etc. are not practiced on Purim. Also difficult for "some say": the mourner for a matter of mitzvah to pray in ten or Kiddush Levanah leaves his house's door — for Mechaber 65 it implies even if he has no minyan at home he does not go out; Rabbenu Yerucham ruled he goes out — publicizing the miracle; also there is no mourning on Purim — if not so no; see Knesset HaGedolah; Eliyah Rabbah 431; and siman 425 for Kiddush Levanah — requires study. One should not read for a mourner, for in public there is no mourning on Purim; see siman 688.
peri-megadim/4:_: Permitted Orach Chayyim on Yom Tov one learns "in your festival" and not "with your wife" — unlike Purim; Magen Avraham letter 18 agreed one may not marry on Purim except canopy on the 13th and feast permitted at night — see there. It implies 14th for walled cities and 15th for villages; perhaps Magen Avraham would concede permitted as siman 695 seif 2 in Hagahah and Orach Chayyim on 14th and 15th one may not marry in name of Mordechai and Mahari Weil — see there.
peri-megadim/5:_: And what Taz wrote: but the custom follows the first view — it refers to what is written in Hagahah they wear etc.; shaatnez d'rabbanan showed a place for the 14th 82; and there in name of Bach one should cook this custom whether on Purim or at wedding joy; and so Beer HaGolah there; it appears when all a man's garments are only one woman's garment and they are recognizable — also for many views on the 14th 82 there is no Torah prohibition such as this; one should not protest on Purim; see Eliyah Rabbah here in name of Shelah: they grab food and there is no theft — it is night of the 13th and day of the 14th and night of the 14th for villages and cities night of the 14th and 15th and night of the 15th. Permitted to bless on food they grab and there is no "one who blesses and seizes"; Shelah wrote it is not from year of chasidim; one who guards his soul should distance; fortunate is one who is careful.
shaarei-teshuvah/1:_: One does [melacha]. Avodat HaTumah; see R' Yehuda in name of Beit David: one who was building his house before Purim through a gentile — since the matter became known, stop on Purim day; see there; it appears there in a place that practiced not to do, even through a gentile; and it is possible he holds building a house in public one should be more stringent — requires study.
turei-zahav/1:_: In all places not to do. It appears merchandise is permitted since it is joy for him; similar to what Beit Yosef wrote in name of Orach Chayyim that one may write a letter, ask of peace, and remind of his debts; and even though regarding Tisha B'Av merchandise is forbidden as written siman 554 — here it is different, for he may do all that is joy for him.
turei-zahav/4:_: And some say mourning does not apply etc. Superficially it implies this "some say" disputes what was written first that he goes to synagogue to hear Megillah — behold at time of prayer he should not go there — this "some say" disputes and holds he may go to synagogue even at time of prayer; and this is not so, for this "some say" is Maharam of Rothenburg whom Tur brought, and wrote there he prays at home and afterward goes to hear — nevertheless; if so this "some say" does not dispute except on what is written that mourning applies on Purim, namely doing mourning acts in public — he holds one should not do so, and going to prayer is forbidden and this is not called public for it is not recognizable he does so because of mourning. It appears to me: since there is no mourning on Purim in public, one should not read in synagogue on Motzei Shabbat before Barchu to walk opposite the mourner, for one should not mention mourner's name in public; rather he goes to synagogue without reading.
turei-zahav/6:_: And as written on the 14th. And since Rama wrote there our custom is to be lenient in asking peace, it is permitted to send him portions too; but it does not appear to rely on this unless the mourner is poor.
yad-ephraim/2:_: Seif 2 exchanging with one another etc. — in gemara it implies villages where there is doubt if walled from days of Yehoshua ben Nun — properly they practiced to forbid on both; see Darkei Moshe in name of Abudraham that even on day two the women practiced not to do.
yad-ephraim/3:_: In Shulchan Aruch seif 4 private matters etc. — in Tashbatz 498 ch. 3 it appears even in private it is not practiced — see there.
yad-ephraim/5:_: In Shulchan Aruch seif 7 like divrei kabbalah. And even though on second day of Yom Tov Mechaber ruled above siman 688 that mourning applies — it must be divrei kabbalah takes precedence; and furthermore it appears what is forbidden in meat and wine is certainly d'rabbanan alone and is deferred before Purim joy which is divrei kabbalah; but requires study, for above he ruled mourning applies and it implies even on other days that are not d'oraisa; and it does not appear to say his intent is this "some say" disputes above; and it is possible his reason is since it already took effect, Purim does not come and defer it, as Ran wrote; if so regarding onen, if his dead died on Purim it is the reverse, aninut does not come and defer Purim's positive mitzvah; but thirty days in Shulchan Aruch do not imply so, for we come on it because of divrei kabbalah like divrei kabbalah — if so Purim should not be deferred even if aninut and mourning preceded. I found one wrote it contradicts; see Tashbatz the aforementioned siman that his view is the essence of Purim feast enactment is only not to fast, and abundance of feast is only d'rabbanan alone; and in Magen Avraham s.k. 15.
yad-ephraim/7:_: In Magen Avraham s.k. 14 what relevance is this — requires study; in my humble opinion one could say Rama holds: since onen is exempt from all mitzvot, nevertheless we see he is not exempt from this mitzvah of Purim joy — all the more he is not exempt from Megillah, prayer, and Shema which are literally d'oraisa; and therefore specifically at night when he does not wish to bury then he is not exempt; requires study, for what is his "all the more" — behold prayer is d'rabbanan; also per this it must be this refers specifically to night, also feast; and difficult is Magen Avraham's question in s.k. 15 — see there.
chokhmat-shlomo/2:_: I finished with God's help today Thursday 10 Adar near the days of Purim. May He guard us from suffering. May the merit of my father the holy gaon ztz"l protect us for generations. May our horn be raised in honor. Year of heavenly mercy for the community. May He live and cause salvation to sprout for the community. And may I merit to spread further his holy books and books with which God favored me in the midst of the day — may we be strengthened for the community.
